record.paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
record.context_brief: Principles for quantum subsystem theories and QTAIM extensions
record.original_question: How should a quantum subsystem, or a division into system plus environment, be introduced when the principles of quantum mechanics do not provide a clear recipe, and how should QTAIM’s own subsystem principles and axioms be extended as part of an ongoing research programme rather than treated as a finalized theory?

evidence.quote: The idea of subsystem is foreign to quantum mechanics and the principles of the theory do not give a clear recipe how a quantum subsystem, or division to system plus environment, must be introduced.

The fact that these theories do not directly flow from the basic principles of quantum mechanics and contain their own principles and axioms give them their own unique identity, distinct from quantum mechanics; this identity includes their mathematical formalism as well as specific capabilities.

All these examples cast doubt that the final chapter of the QTAIM has been written yet and as proposed recently [27,38,79], the QTAIM must be seen as an ongoing “research programme” rather than a “finalized theory”.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In standard quantum mechanics, a closed system is described by a state vector (or density operator) on a Hilbert space, evolving unitarily under a Hamiltonian; the theory's basic postulates do not, by themselves, single out a canonical decomposition of a given system into a "subsystem" together with an "environment." The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) introduces such a decomposition for a molecular system by partitioning real space into disjoint regions Ω bounded by zero-flux surfaces of the gradient field of the one-electron density ρ(r), i.e. open regions Ω ⊂ ℝ³ whose boundary ∂Ω satisfies ∇ρ(r)·n(r) = 0 for all r ∈ ∂Ω, with n(r) the outward unit normal. To each such region one associates subsystem observables (e.g. the atomic energy, atomic populations, and atomic action obtained by integrating appropriate densities over Ω) and a subsystem variational principle generalizing Schwinger's principle of stationary action.

Formulate, in a mathematically precise way, a foundational framework that addresses the following:

(a) Provide a set of axioms specifying when, and in what mathematical sense, a closed quantum system described on a Hilbert space ℋ together with a Hamiltonian H admits a well-defined decomposition into a "subsystem" and a "complementary environment," in such a way that the subsystem carries its own observables, state, and dynamics consistent with (but not derivable from) the standard postulates of quantum mechanics.

(b) Within this framework, extend the existing QTAIM subsystem principles—zero-flux boundary condition, atomic variational principle, and atomic expectation values defined through integrals over zero-flux regions—into a complete and self-consistent set of axioms for a quantum theory of spatial subsystems of a many-electron system, identifying the additional principles (beyond those of quantum mechanics) that are required and proving their internal consistency.

(c) Determine whether the resulting theory can be developed as an open-ended research programme, in the sense that one specifies a hard core of fixed axioms together with a class of admissible extensions (e.g. to time-dependent, relativistic, or open-system settings), and characterize precisely the scope and limits of such extensions.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is foundational and programmatic, asking for a mathematical/axiomatic framework for quantum subsystems and an extension of QTAIM's axioms. No definitive resolution is reported in the literature; QTAIM is generally still regarded as an evolving research programme with active discussion of its foundations, so the problem is best classified as open.

status_evidence.title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of QTAIM as an ongoing research programme with open foundational problems regarding the notion of quantum subsystem.
status_evidence.claim: The foundational status of quantum subsystems and QTAIM extensions is presented as an open programme rather than a settled theory.
